Inbound QoS 2 is tracked symmetrically — db__message_insert_incoming, L468 holds the publisher’s message until PUBREL completes the handshake. Because sessions matter more than any single message, delivery state is designed to survive restarts: persist__backup, L344 serializes clients, subscriptions, retained messages and in-flight queues into the persistence file, and persist__restore, L419 replays it at boot — with dedicated legacy readers (persist_read_v234.c) for old database formats and re-arming of MQTT 5 session expiry timers from persisted data. The db_dump app (main, L455) exists to inspect that file offline.

Security is just plugins

The same registry that carries password checks also carries everything else. mosquitto_security_init_default, L32 boots the built-in providers: the ACL file (broker_acl_file__init, L32) and the password file. MQTT 5 enhanced authentication routes AUTH packets to extended-auth plugins via handle__auth, L33. The flagship example ships in-tree: the dynamic-security plugin (mosquitto_plugin_init, L56) registers auth, ACL and control callbacks so clients, roles and groups can be managed while the broker runs — an administrator publishes commands to $CONTROL/dynamic-security/v1 (response topic defined at L31), dynsec__handle_command, L34 applies them, and replies go back through the broker-facing plugin API mosquitto_broker_publish, L213. Plugins also receive a periodic tick (plugin__handle_tick, L58) and message-in/out hooks, so an ACL decision never has to be hard-coded in the dispatch path.

From passwd files to dynamic security: the build facts

The repository builds one broker and a supporting toolkit. Version 2.1.2 is set in CMakeLists.txt, L9; the project carries dual build systems (CMake and classic Make). Four apps ship under apps/: mosquitto_passwd (main, L436) hashes password-file entries, mosquitto_ctrl drives the control topics, db_dump reads persistence files, and mosquitto_signal nudges a running broker. Under plugins/ there is the ACL-file plugin, dynamic security, and examples ranging from auth-by-ip to add-properties. Transports go beyond raw TCP: websockets.c runs the same dispatch over MQTT-in-WebSockets, selected per transport in the epoll reader (L271–274). Brokers bridge to brokers: bridge.c plus bridge_check() in the main loop keeps remote topic prefixes synchronized. The historical arc is visible in the layout — static files (acl_file.c, password_file.c) parsed at startup versus the dynamic-security plugin editing state at runtime — and it mirrors ecosystem reality: Node-RED flows and new Zigbee devices appear far more often than anyone edits a config file, so the manage-it-live path is the one that scaled. Files carry dual SPDX headers (EPL-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause), and ChangeLog.txt documents each release.

Honest Limits

  • One process, one core for packet work. There is no clustering code in the repository; the $SYS tree is per-process, and scaling means running more brokers and bridging them, not adding threads.
  • Persistence is a snapshot, not a journal. persist__backup runs on the autosave_interval/change-count logic in the main loop (L225–238); a crash can lose up to one interval of persistence changes.
  • QoS 2 costs four packets end-to-end. The dispatch switch shows the full PUBLISH → PUBREC → PUBREL → PUBCOMP chain (L60–66); durability is paid per message.
  • Retained state is last-value-per-topic, not history. retain__store replaces or clears (L189); there is no replay of past messages.
  • File-based auth is startup-time. ACL and password files are parsed at init and on reload; clients cannot change them live — that capability is exactly what the dynamic-security plugin adds.
  • Line numbers refer to master at HEAD fda14f2c196d (2026-11-15), version 2.1.2 development, and will drift; the architecture is the durable part. And when a workload outgrows a single broker’s pub/sub semantics — queues, cluster consensus, multi-region fan-out — servers like NATS make the opposite trade-off, buying distribution at the cost of the tiny-single-binary simplicity Mosquitto optimizes for.
entry.summary: How Mosquitto works: source tour of the C MQTT broker's single-threaded event loop, topic tree routing, QoS message store, persistence, and plugin auth layer.

entry.title: How Node-RED Works: Inside the Flow Engine and Runtime Architecture

link.title: How Node-RED Works: Inside the Flow Engine and Runtime Architecture

entry.content:
Every smart home starts the same way: a Python script polling one vendor API, a cron job pushing to another, a MQTT subscriber copied from a blog post, and a folder of half-finished glue scripts nobody dares to delete. Each integration works alone, none of them share state, and when one throws an exception at 3 a.m. the others keep running blind. Node-RED’s core idea was to make the wiring itself the artifact — drag nodes onto a canvas, connect them into a flow, press Deploy — but the reason it survived a decade of alternatives is the runtime underneath: a tiny, disciplined engine that routes messages between nodes with predictable semantics, persists flows to disk, and restarts exactly the pieces you changed.

This post walks that engine in the real source (node-red/node-red, branch main, HEAD e4f7fc516cd8, checked 2026-11-15) with two generated call graphs. The overview shows the moving parts: the CLI bootstrap, the editor API and its WebSocket channel, the runtime API layer, the flow engine, the node registry, and the context stores. The detail view goes one level deeper — the deploy cycle from POST /flows to running flows, and the full journey of one message from node.send() to the next node’s input callback.

By the end you will know where a Deploy button click actually lands in code, why a fan-out to five branches clones the message but a linear chain does not, how context.get("myvar") finds its store, and why the runtime mounts two separate express apps on two separate URL roots. The story is a good companion to our earlier Domoticz tour — two very different answers to the same home-automation problem.

Overview: the CLI boots lib/red.js, which wires the runtime and the editor API into one express server; the editor talks to the runtime through an admin REST API plus a WebSocket bus; the flow manager instantiates Flow objects that route messages between Node instances resolved from the registry.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Bootstrap is two packages wired together by hand. init, L57 receives the HTTP server from the CLI, then calls runtime.init, L73 and api.init, L75 in sequence and merges the two express apps with api.httpAdmin.use(runtime.httpAdmin), L77. There is no service locator — just three requires at L20–23 and a handful of function calls.
  • The runtime start chain is an explicit promise chain of subsystems. start, L135 registers the i18n catalog, then initializes storage, settings, telemetry, library and multiplayer (L136–141), loads node types with redNodes.load(), L166 and only then loads and starts the flows (L241–244). Order matters: no node types exist before the registry loads, and no flows run before contexts are ready.
  • One process, two express apps, two URL roots. nodeApp and adminApp are created at L94–95; the CLI mounts adminApp at httpAdminRoot (L423) and nodeApp at httpNodeRoot (L435). That separation is why your HTTP-in endpoints can sit behind different auth and a different path prefix than the editor.
  • send is optimized by wiring shape. updateWires, L89 inspects the wires array: an unwired node gets its send replaced by NOOP_SEND, L101, and a node with exactly one output and one target gets a cached _wire, L107 so the hot path skips all iteration.
  • One message hop is a SendEvent flowing through hook stages. Node.send, L381 builds an array of send events — one per output-per-wire — and hands them to this._flow.send, L491; Flow.send, L715 runs onSend → preRoute → preDeliver hooks (handleOnSend, L790). Cloning is precise: the clone flag is set only from the second send onward (L466), and preRoute clones per branch when needed (L813–815).
  • Delivery is deferred by exactly one tick. handlePreDeliver, L831 wraps delivery in setImmediate, L839 unless runtimeSyncDelivery forces synchronous mode (L858). Deep chains therefore never recurse through the stack — each hop is a fresh macrotask.
  • The editor talks REST plus WebSocket, not one or the other. Flow CRUD rides the admin API (GET/POST /flows, L43–44); live traffic — status updates, notifications, debug messages — rides a WebSocket server attached via server.on('upgrade'), L237 at <adminRoot>/comms, with per-connection sends batched on a 50 ms timer (_queueSend, L192).
  • The runtime mirrors internal events back to every editor. publish, L77 fans node-status and runtime-event emissions out to all connections, keeping a retained map that replays on subscribe (L153–163). This is why a second browser tab sees the same node status dots as the first.
  • Node types are a registry, filled by a disk scanner. load, L36 asks the local-filesystem module for node sets in core dirs and the userDir node_modules tree; registerNodeConstructor, L435 rejects duplicate type names and emits type-registered (L461) — the event that unblocks flows sitting on missing types.

Detail view: the deploy path (editor → admin routes → mutex-guarded flows API → diff, save, stop, start) on the left, and the message path (Node.send → flow hook stages → setImmediate → receive → input callback → done) on the right, with the registry and context stores underneath.

The deploy cycle: from editor click to running flows

When you press Deploy, the editor sends POST /flows with a Node-RED-Deployment-Type header — full, nodes, flows, or reload (L50). The runtime API layer serializes everything behind an async-mutex, L37 so two concurrent deploys cannot interleave (setFlows, L66–67). Optimistic concurrency is built in: if the editor’s rev does not match the active revision, the deploy fails with version_mismatch and HTTP 409 (L78–84) — that is the “another user has modified your flows” dialog reduced to five lines.

The real work happens in setFlows, L118: the config is cloned, parsed, and compared against the active config via diffConfigs, L154, which classifies every node as added, changed, removed, rewired, or linked. Credentials are exported and the whole config is written through storage.saveFlows, L202 before anything is restarted. Only then does the manager stop, L220 the affected flows, clean up orphaned context (L222), and start, L228 the new config.

The deploy type determines the blast radius. A full deploy creates a Flow object for the global config (L357) plus one per tab (L365); a modified-nodes or modified-flows deploy calls update on the flows that changed, L385–390 and leaves untouched tabs running. Each surviving await activeFlows[id].start(diff), L402 then rebuilds only what the diff says: new nodes are instantiated, rewired nodes just get updateWires applied, and closed nodes run their close callbacks under a 15-second timeout (stopNode, L768–778).

Inside one message hop: node.send to the next input

Follow one message through the detail diagram. (1) The sending node’s send, L381 stamps a fresh _msgid on first send (L397–399), takes the single-wire shortcut when possible (L393–414), and otherwise walks every output and wire building SendEvents (L429–475). (2) Flow.send runs the hook stages: onSend once for the batch (L792), preRoute per event, which resolves the destination via flow.getNode, L811 and clones the message for fan-out branches. (3) preDeliver schedules the hand-off inside setImmediate, L838–841. (4) deliverMessageToDestination, L821 calls destination.node.receive(msg). (5) receive, L499 stamps _msgid if missing and emits input, which routes into _emitInput, L201: the onReceive hook fires first (L206), then your node’s callback runs as input(msg, send, done) (L214–218).

The done callback is the modern completion contract. Calling done() routes through _complete, L132, which triggers the onComplete hook and asks the flow to notify any complete nodes wired downstream (handleComplete, L698); calling done(err) instead goes to handleError, L596, which dispatches to catch nodes. Errors thrown synchronously inside the input callback are caught and logged rather than crashing the process (L219–221). Because every hop lands in a fresh macrotask, this design composes cleanly with the event loop — if you want the underlying model, our Node.js event loop walkthrough covers the mechanics this engine leans on. Node-RED adds one hard backstop on top: an uncaught exception anywhere still terminates the whole process (red.js, L525–541).

Context: where flow state actually lives

Node-RED gives every node three context scopes — node-local, flow, and global — and the implementation is lazier than you might expect. Node.prototype.context(), L119 creates the node’s context object on first use, keyed by nodeId:flowId (getContext, L520), and attaches flow and global as read-only properties (L540–546). Flow-level contexts are created in the Flow constructor itself (L64), with $parent traversal for subflow nesting.

Which store backs those lookups is a settings decision. load, L69 reads settings.contextStorage, instantiates each configured plugin, and lets a key name pick a store inline — context.get("cache","myredis") style, where parseContextStore splits the store from the key (L299–302). The default is the Memory store, L19: a plain object per scope, fast and intentionally non-persistent. Everything else — file-backed, or third-party stores such as a Redis connector for cross-restart shared state — plugs into the same two-method interface. During a deploy, orphaned contexts are pruned by clean, L591 against the known node set, and the admin API exposes /context/:scope/:id read routes (L79–82) so you can inspect live state without adding a debug node.

From single-file demo to a v5 monorepo

The repository shape tells the maturity story. Since the 1.x restructure, the code is a pnpm-style monorepo under packages/node_modules/: @node-red/runtime, @node-red/editor-api, @node-red/registry, @node-red/util, @node-red/nodes (the core node set — inject, debug, function, catch, template and friends), @node-red/editor-client (the browser editor source), and a thin node-red CLI wrapper on top. The root package.json names the whole thing node-red at version 5.0.9, L2–3, marked private because the packages are published individually, and hard-pins the runtime: "node": ">=22.9", L134. The CLI enforces the same floor twice — once with semver.satisfies, L30 and again inside lib/red.js — and refuses to start otherwise.

First-run ergonomics are equally concrete. With no settings file found, the CLI copies its bundled default settings.js into ~/.node-red — but only if the default has not been modified on disk, checked by comparing mtime against ctime (L149–156) — so upgrades never silently overwrite your config. The same binary doubles as an admin client: node-red admin ... short-circuits into the node-red-admin package (L18–27). And for embedded use, running with both HTTP roots disabled logs server.headless-mode and skips server.listen entirely (L513–515) — the engine still runs flows, just with no network surface. Test hygiene matches the split: unit tests are separated into mocha:core and mocha:nodes suites (package.json, L20–22), and linting covers only the editor client sources (L17).

Honest Limits

  • Line numbers drift. Everything above was verified against main at HEAD e4f7fc516cd8 (2026-11-15); the architecture is durable, the line anchors are not.
  • The core node set here is small on purpose. The repo ships @node-red/nodes/core (common, function, sequence, parser, network, storage groups), but the hundreds of palette nodes — MQTT brokers, GPIO, dashboard widgets — are separate npm modules resolved from userDir/node_modules at load time (loader.js, L36–44). Reading this repo will not show you how your specific third-party node behaves.
  • One process, one point of failure. All flows run in a single Node process; the uncaughtException handler logs and calls process.exit(1) (red.js, L525–541). There is no per-flow isolation, no worker threads, no failover in this codebase.
  • The default context store is volatile. Unless you configure contextStorage, all context lives in a plain JavaScript object and vanishes on restart (memory.js, L19–21). Persistence is a configuration step, not a default.
  • This post skips subflow internals. Subflow.js instances wrap the same Node machinery with aliasing (_alias in Node.js, L50–52), but instance creation and env inheritance in Subflow.js deserve their own tour.
entry.summary: Node-RED internals from source: the runtime core, node registry, message passing between nodes, context stores, admin API vs HTTP nodes, and the deploy cycle.

entry.title: How OctoPrint Works: Inside the 3D Print Server Architecture

link.title: How OctoPrint Works: Inside the 3D Print Server Architecture

entry.content:
A five-hour print job used to mean five hours of pretending to watch a machine: hover over the USB cable, pray the bed adhesion holds, walk back to the garage at 2 a.m. to see whether the part fan is still spinning. Every hobbyist who has babysitted a printer this way knows the moment the idea clicks — the printer should behave like every other appliance in the house. That is the shift OctoPrint delivers, and it is the same jump that turned home-automation boxes like Domoticz from geek projects into genuinely useful appliances: one small always-on computer, a browser, and the printer becomes something you check from the couch instead of something you stand next to.

But OctoPrint is not a firmware. It never runs on the printer’s mainboard. It is a full Python server that lives on a Raspberry Pi next to the machine, and its internals are worth reading because they solve a genuinely hard problem: keeping a fragile serial link to a chatty, protocol-less device alive for hours while a dozen browser tabs watch. The two diagrams below map that architecture. The overview shows the shape of the system at boot — how one Server object composes the plugin runtime, the file handling, the print state machine and the event bus. The detail graph follows a G-code byte from a browser click or a file upload down to the serial port and back up as live state pushed to every connected client.

After this tour you can answer the questions that matter when you hack on OctoPrint or steal its ideas: where plugins get loaded and why the serial driver is itself a plugin, how the server survives a printer that sends garbage mid-print, how state reaches browsers every half a second, and where the REST API, real-time push and the event bus cross paths.

Figure 1 — OctoPrint overview architecture: one Server.run composes the plugin runtime, print state machine, serial link, file handling and the event bus that everything else hangs off.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The composition root is a single method. Server.run, L317 assigns every global singleton the rest of the system reads — printer, fileManager, analysisQueue, eventManager, pluginManager. No dependency injection; the globals are the service locator, and everything hangs off them.
  • Plugins load before the web stack starts. PluginManager, L835 discovers plugins from setuptools entry points and folders, wrapping each hit in a PluginInfo, L325 metadata object. Serving HTTP before plugin discovery finishes is not an option the design allows.
  • One blueprint per API domain. The core REST module exposes login(), L324 and version info, while job, files, connection and printer commands live in separate route modules — a clean per-domain split rather than one mega-router.
  • Printer connectors form a registry. ConnectedPrinter, L229 uses a registration metaclass: any subclass registers itself on definition, and find() resolves a connector by name. The core never hardcodes how to reach a printer.
  • The serial engine is a plugin. MachineCom, L486 — roughly 7,000 lines of serial protocol handling — lives in the bundled serial_connector plugin. The old core path comm.py, L3 is now just a deprecation shim re-exporting from the plugin.
  • One facade owns all print state. Printer, L79 holds every job transition the UI can trigger: set_job, L823, start_print, L905, pause_print, L936 and cancel_print, L969.
  • Files flow through a storage-agnostic manager. An upload lands via FileManager.add_file, L778 across local disk or SD card storages, then the GcodeAnalysisQueue, L361 walks the G-code in the background to estimate print time and filament use before you ever press start.
  • Browsers get half-second pushes, not polling. Each connected client gets a PrinterStateConnection, L74 — a SockJS session that receives on_printer_send_current_data, L403 callbacks and streams state, temperatures and logs straight to the UI.
  • Everything crosses the event bus. EventManager.fire, L216 is the pub-sub hub for the Events constants, L29 — from Startup to PrinterStateChanged — that decouple the web tier, the printer tier and plugins.

Figure 2 — OctoPrint detail architecture: from REST routes and the per-browser SockJS session down through the connector registry into MachineCom's monitor loop and send queues, plus the file, analysis and event subsystems around it.

Why OctoPrint Is a Server, Not a Firmware Add-On

OctoPrint’s code lives in one package, src/octoprint, and the class that owns the boot sequence is Server, L266 in server/__init__.py. Its run() method does something unusual for a Python web app: it writes a safe-mode flag file before doing anything risky (L318), so a crash mid-startup is detected on the next boot and the server comes back in a limited safe mode instead of half-alive.

The web layer is two servers stacked. Flask produces the REST surface — thin route modules under server/api — while Tornado fronts it as the raw HTTP engine: CustomHTTPServer, L1070 wraps the WSGI app, and the same module carries large-file download handlers and webcam snapshot endpoints. The split will feel familiar from our Django internals tour: keep HTTP plumbing disposable, keep domain logic in services that never import web code. That separation is why plugins can hook into printing without touching a single route.

Real-time is not an afterthought bolted onto Flask. During boot the server registers a SockJS route at /sockjs (L2038) and builds one PrinterStateConnection per browser (L2806). The session object is both a push channel and an event listener, so the live temperature graphs and progress bars in the UI ride that single socket rather than hammering the REST API with polls.

The Plugin Manager Runs Before Anything Else

Before any web machinery starts, PluginManager, L835 must finish. It scans entry points and plugin folders, wraps each candidate in PluginInfo, L325, and only then hands out validated implementations. Under the hood this is standard CPython machinery — importlib and entry-point metadata; our CPython source tour covers what those imports trigger.

What makes the design sing is plugin/types.py: about 2,700 lines of mixin classes every plugin composes. OctoPrintPlugin, L26 is the base; BlueprintPlugin, L1439 registers a plugin’s own Flask blueprint; EventHandlerPlugin, L2316 subscribes to the event bus; SettingsPlugin, L1729 contributes a settings schema. A plugin declares capabilities by choosing mixins, and the core discovers what it can do at runtime instead of checking version flags.

The best proof that the core trusts this contract: the serial driver is itself a bundled plugin. Twenty-one bundled plugins ship in-tree — softwareupdate, pluginmanager, virtual_printer, gcodeviewer, discovery, tracking among them — so the plugin interface is exercised by the project itself on every boot. The comm layer is the newest member: octoprint.util.comm moved wholesale into plugins/serial_connector, leaving only the shim.

How a G-code Line Reaches the Heater

Follow one print command downward. The REST endpoint controlJob(), L20 ends in Printer.start_print(); a connection command from connectionCommand(), L139 lands in Printer.connect, L446. Connect is where the plugin architecture earns its keep: registered connect hooks get first refusal (L464), a CONNECTING event fires for everyone listening (L482), and only then does ConnectedPrinter.find() (L486) resolve the named connector — by default "serial" — into a live object.

Inside the serial plugin, ConnectedSerialPrinter, L38 bridges the core’s callback interface to MachineCom, L486. A background monitor loop (_monitor(), L2337) sits in a readline loop (_readline(), L4319) classifying every incoming line: temperature reports, acknowledgements, resend requests, error messages. Outgoing G-code never blocks the caller — it is queued in SendQueue, L6348 and drained at the pace the printer actually acknowledges. Job files stream line by line through StreamingGcodeFileInformation, L6247. The printer never waits for the network; the network never waits for the printer.

The Print State Machine and Its Half-Second Heartbeat

All that serial chatter converges upward on one object: the Printer facade. Each transition — job set, started, paused, cancelled — fires events through the bus, and the StateMonitor, L2058 built with a 0.5-second interval (L174) runs the heartbeat: every half second it invokes _send_current_data_callbacks, L343, which copies the state dictionary and hands it to every registered listener — the SockJS session among them. That single callback chain is why the UI progress bar moves smoothly while the serial link is busy.

Estimation runs on two clocks. Before a print, the analysis queue’s GcodeAnalysisQueue, L361 drives gcode, L226 — a model-aware parser that walks every line to compute duration, filament usage and object bounds. During a print, PrintTimeEstimator, L9 refines the number from observed line timing, because a printer’s real speed depends on firmware settings the G-code cannot predict. The analysis result even flows back through the bus: the queue fires MetadataAnalysisFinished (L144) and the printer facade subscribes to it (L209).

From Core Monolith to Plugin Space: Build Facts

The repository tells a story about where the project is heading:

  • One Python package, src/octoprint, holds the core: access, cli, filemanager, printer, server, slicing, util, plugin and the bundled plugins tree.
  • The recent structural shift moved serial communication from octoprint/util/comm.py into the bundled serial_connector plugin, leaving only the deprecation shim in core. Expect more subsystems to follow.
  • serial_comm.py is the largest file in the package at roughly 7,200 lines; plugin/types.py follows at about 2,700.
  • The event bus is small but load-bearing: events.py defines the constants, lets admins bind shell commands to events via CommandTrigger, L326, and powers features like timelapse recording through TimelapseRenderJob, L1087.
  • Access control is a first-class subsystem, not an afterthought: Permissions, L270 is a metaclass-backed registry, and the default FilebasedUserManager, L410 ships with the core.
  • The dev branch carries an in-flight API v2: connection state routes exist twice (connectionState, L93 and connectionState_2_0_0, L114) during the migration.

Honest Limits

  • The connector registry is general, but only one connector ships. ConnectedPrinter.find() can resolve any registered transport, yet the bundled tree contains exactly one serial implementation — Bluetooth, network or other transports are architecture-shaped holes, not features.
  • Metadata analysis only understands G-code. The queue’s own docstring says so (L57: “At the moment, only gcode is supported here”), so STL-to-print-time estimation does not exist in the core.
  • The push channel is SockJS, not raw WebSockets: the server vendors sockjs.min.js so clients on flaky networks get fallback transports, at protocol overhead a plain WebSocket would not carry.
  • Safe mode is detection, not recovery. The boot flag written at L318 gets the server into a diagnostic state after a failed start; it does not repair a broken config for you.
  • The diagrams are a reading aid, not the code: callback chains are simplified, and the linked source is the truth.
entry.summary: OctoPrint turned 3D printers into networked appliances. Tour the Python server internals: plugin manager, serial G-code comm, print state machine, event bus.

entry.title: How openHAB Works: Inside the OSGi Smart Home Core Architecture

link.title: How openHAB Works: Inside the OSGi Smart Home Core Architecture

entry.content:
Ask anyone who has owned two smart home hubs why they replaced the first one, and the answer is rarely the hardware: it is the model. Every hub invents its own vocabulary for “a lamp,” ships its own rules language, and refuses to talk to the neighbors’ protocols — so your Z-Wave stick, your Hue bridge and your MQTT sensors each need a separate integration with a separate device model, and when a vendor sunsets a hub the whole abstraction dies with it. openHAB’s bet, refined over fifteen years, is that this problem is structural: put one device model and one event bus inside a Java process, and make every driver a replaceable module around them.

That bet is visible in the repository this post walks: openhab/openhab-core, branch main at HEAD 15c6da97b24e (checked 2026-11-15), roughly 100 OSGi bundle modules and 2,550 Java files of pure framework — no device drivers, no UI chrome. Two generated architecture graphs accompany the text: an overview of the moving parts, then a detail view of the wiring that carries one command from a UI toggle to a device handler and one state change back.

By the end you will know where a button press becomes an event, how an item command finds the right handler through a profile indirection, how the rule engine runs composable trigger/condition/action graphs, why discovered devices land in an inbox before they become Things, and what the OSGi module system buys that a plain monolithic framework would not.

Overview: the org.openhab.core base bundle declares the Item and Event contracts; the thing bundle models devices plus their handlers; CommunicationManager routes item commands and updates through per-link profiles; everything crosses one OSGi EventAdmin event bus; the rule engine and discovery hang off the same bus.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The device model is three small interfaces, not a class hierarchy. Thing, L42 is documented as “a representation of a connected part (e.g. physical device or cloud service)” and amounts to channels, configuration, status and properties (getChannels(), L82). Channel, L42 carries the item type it accepts plus a kind (getKind(), L107) that separates state channels from trigger channels, and Bridge extends Thing, L28 lets a hub host child Things.
  • Nothing calls a device driver directly — everything rides one event bus. OSGiEventPublisher, L38 implements the openHAB EventPublisher, L24 contract by wrapping the standard OSGi EventAdmin and posting every event on a single "openhab" topic (eventAdmin.postEvent(...), L69). On the receive side, OSGiEventManager, L44 declares "event.topics:String=openhab", deserializes payloads through registered factories, and fans out to each EventSubscriber.receive(), L58 that subscribed to the event type.
  • Items and Things are decoupled on purpose. Item, L38 never mentions devices: it is state plus accepted command types (getState(), L45). The join point is ItemChannelLink, L29 — an item name plus getLinkedUID(), L57 — and CommunicationManager, L97 implements both EventSubscriber and the link-registry change listener, keeping a per-link profile cache warm (L204).
  • Commands cross exactly one transform layer: profiles. A configured link can pin a profile (getConfiguredProfileTypeUID, L228); otherwise advisors and the system default factory decide (L246). The default profile ends the trip at onCommandFromItem, L377, which lands in the handler’s handleCommand(ChannelUID, Command), L101 — the one method every binding must implement.
  • The framework, not the binding, owns the lifecycle. ThingRegistryImpl, L55 notifies all ThingTrackers on every add or update (L213); ThingManagerImpl, L124 picks the factory whose supportsThingType(), L40 matches, calls registerHandler(Thing), L55, and runs doInitializeHandler(), L737 under SafeCaller timeout guards — a hung binding degrades one Thing, not the process.
  • States come back as events, with a policy for self-echo. A handler’s updateState(), L324 becomes an ItemStateEvent on the topic template openhab/items/{itemName}/state (L54), while commands on openhab/items/{itemName}/command (L52) pass through AutoUpdateManager.receiveCommand(), L138, which can echo the command as state when the channel declares an auto-update policy.
  • Rules are data: composable modules that subscribe like everyone else. A Rule, L47 is a graph of Trigger, L41, Condition, L43 and Action, L42 modules held in RuleEngineImpl, L125’s concurrent map (L146). Event triggers are ordinary subscribers: GenericEventTriggerHandler, L49 implements EventSubscriber, and a match calls triggered(), L54, which submits to a per-rule sequential executor running re.runRule() (L86).
  • Discovery ends in an inbox, never straight in the registry. Bindings implement DiscoveryService.startScan(), L114; results fan out via thingDiscovered(), L359; the PersistentInbox, L96 stores proposals, and only the explicit approve(), L187 materializes a managed Thing.

Detail view: ThingRegistryImpl pushes tracker callbacks into ThingManagerImpl, which wires handler factories to per-device handlers; CommunicationManager resolves profiles per ItemChannelLink; the OSGi event bus connects items, rule triggers and the discovery inbox into one async fabric.

One bus, two object worlds

The design’s pivotal choice is that the “functional” world (Items, what users automate) and the “physical” world (Things, what bindings drive) never hold references to each other. ItemChannelLink, L29 is the entire bridge, and the ItemChannelLinkRegistry, L74 tracks it so relinking an item to a different channel is a registry mutation, not a code change. Consequences show up everywhere: renaming a device requires no UI edits, one item can draw state from several Things, and the same link table powers REST and UI alike.

The bus underneath is deliberately in-process. OSGiEventPublisher hands events to the OSGi EventAdmin running inside the JVM; there is no broker hop between a UI command and a device handler, which is why command latency is a thread schedule rather than a network round trip. If you need fan-out across machines you bring your own transport — the same trade-off we examined when comparing Redis pub/sub to local queues: in-process buses win on latency and lose on topology, and openHAB chose latency, then layered transports (MQTT, Modbus, serial) as separate bundles for the edges that genuinely speak protocols.

What a binding must actually provide

A binding author writes three things: a ThingHandler with handleCommand() and initialize(), a ThingHandlerFactory that claims its Thing types, and XML descriptions under OH-INF/ that the repo’s XML providers parse into ThingType/ChannelType objects — ThingType, L41 lists channel definitions, config parameters and supported bridges. BaseThingHandler, L69 supplies the conveniences (updateState(), updateStatus()) so driver code stays about the device, not the plumbing. Notably, this core repository contains zero device bindings — it ships the SPI, the transports and the marketplace installer machinery; the hundreds of protocol bindings are built elsewhere against these exact interfaces. That is how a bridge like Zigbee2MQTT can be consumed from openHAB without any core change: its MQTT topics are just another client of the MQTT transport bundle, one link table away from ordinary Items.

Rules are graphs, scripts are modules

The automation bundle models rules as connection graphs: trigger outputs feed condition and action inputs by name, with a separator constant (OUTPUT_SEPARATOR, L130) encoding moduleId.outputId references. The engine refuses to run a rule until every module type resolves and every handler attaches, exposing statuses like uninitialized and idle (documented on RuleEngineImpl, L107–113). Script actions (the model.script bundles) are just another module handler type plugged into the same graph — which is why a rule can mix a declarative trigger with a JavaScript action without the engine knowing either syntax. Disabled rules persist separately (DISABLED_RULE_STORAGE, L132) so a restart never resurrects something a user explicitly switched off.

From Eclipse SmartHome to 100 OSGi bundles

The lineage is written in the code. Comments still reference the Eclipse SmartHome tracker (NetUtil.java, L206), and several files carry “port to Eclipse SmartHome” author tags — the project was the Eclipse incubation that openHAB industrialized, and the package roots were renamed org.eclipse.smarthome → org.openhab.core along the way. The build mechanics reflect that OSGi heritage: the README describes the repo as “an artifact repository of OSGi bundles that can be used within smart home products” (L16) whose Maven build “produces OSGi bundles, dependency BOMs … and Karaf feature definitions” (L20). Concretely: 100 bundle modules under bundles/, each a bnd-built OSGi jar; the Karaf feature catalog at feature.xml, L20 assembles openhab-core-base, with transports like openhab-core-io-transport-mqtt, L280 and the rule DSL runtime openhab-core-model-rule, L346 as opt-in features. The version is 5.3.0-SNAPSHOT (pom.xml, L15) under EPL-2.0, and 27 itests/ modules boot real OSGi runtimes from itest.bndrun files (README L38) rather than mocking the registry — which is why service-wiring regressions get caught before release.

Standing next to its neighbors

Compared with Domoticz, which opts for a compact C++ core with Lua/Python scripting, openHAB trades binary weight for a formally versioned extension contract: bindings are OSGi bundles whose compatibility the framework checks, not plugins compiled against a moving header. Compared with Home Assistant, the difference is the same one the diagrams show — openHAB centralizes the event fabric in the runtime and keeps protocol handling in drivers, so the hub process itself stays protocol-agnostic. And for the radio layer, pairing this framework with a bridge such as Zigbee2MQTT keeps the two architectures cleanly separated: openHAB owns modeling and rules; the bridge owns mesh management.

Honest Limits

  • No device drivers ship here. The 100 bundles/ modules are framework, model and transport code; protocol integrations live in the separate add-ons repository, so this source tour explains the contract, not a specific device’s decoding.
  • The event bus is in-JVM only. OSGiEventManager subscribes to OSGi event.topics=openhab inside one process (L44); nothing under org.openhab.core.events serializes events off-box, and remote scenarios are left to separate bundles and deployments.
  • Discovery is binding-dependent. startScan() implementations live with each binding; core only defines the contract (L48) and the inbox, so scan coverage varies per protocol.
  • The rule DSL is part of this repo, but engines for scripts are layered. model.rule/model.script are Xtext language bundles in-tree; their runtime behavior depends on script engines registered as module handlers, which core does not provide.
  • All line numbers refer to main at HEAD 15c6da97b24e (2026-11-15) and will drift as files evolve; the architecture, not the line numbers, is the durable part.
entry.summary: How openHAB works: a source tour of openhab-core's OSGi bundles — Thing/Channel/Item model, binding SPI, EventAdmin event bus, rule engine and discovery.
